- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) over recent days, reduce forecast slope and avoid upward momentum; model tends to overcorrect after negative sentiment.
- If sentiment spikes to 1.00 or 0.67 near the end of history, model often overestimates future prices — cap forecast growth at 1–2% above recent mean if sentiment is bullish.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots — apply a 1–3 day lag correction or reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.00–0.33) and history shows volatility, model tends to underestimate downside risk — add 2–5% buffer for downward moves in next 5–10 days.
- If forecast is flat or trending upward but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 3–7 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from model in first 5–7 days, adjust forecast to align with recent 7-day moving average if sentiment is neutral or mildly bullish.
